subject: A25CD3C8159CEB118B7B8E04471AF21A
introduction: Between 1905 and 1911 Persia demanded a constitution, won a parliament, and fell into civil war and foreign occupation. These are ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s letters and remarks from those years. He says that constitutional government is what divine law intends and that absolute power is contrary to it; that from the first day he told both sides they must blend “like milk and honey” or ruin the country; that Bahá’ís must take no part in the quarrel, and were blamed by each faction as partisans of the other; that clerics and agitators misused the name of freedom; and that calm would return. The constitutional idea has ancient company: the king of Deuteronomy who must copy out the law, Samuel’s warning, Montesquieu and Locke. The reconciling voice has Lincoln’s and Jefferson’s. The disillusion has Wordsworth’s dawn and Yeats’s falling centre. Against the readings stand Douglass, for whom there is no progress without agitation, the Declaration’s right of a people to alter its government, and Peter’s “we ought to obey God rather than men”.
questions: Deuteronomy puts the king under the law, and reading 3 calls constitutional government the kind that conforms to divine law. How does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá combine approval of the aim with refusal to join the struggle?
Douglass says that those who want reform without agitation want crops without ploughing. What do the readings think agitation cost Persia, and is his objection answered?
Lincoln said “we are not enemies, but friends”, and war came. What can a counsel of reconciliation accomplish when both sides refuse it?
Readings 28 and 29 judge the movement by its leaders’ motives, and Tacitus by what conquerors call their work. How should one weigh a cause against those who use its name?
“It would have been better to proceed slowly” (36), and “how is it possible … suddenly” (35). What do the readings imply must be built before a constitution can hold?

outside.why: Government and people “must blend together like milk and honey”. Lincoln, on the eve of civil war: we are not enemies, but friends; we must not be enemies.
Otherwise progress is impossible. If a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand.
“We never interfered.” Jeremiah’s letter to exiles living under a foreign king: seek the peace of the city, and pray unto the Lord for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
A government that conforms to divine law “is a constitutional government”. In Deuteronomy the king must copy out the law and read it all his days, that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren.
And absolute power is contrary to it. Samuel’s warning of the manner of the king: he will take your sons, your fields, the tenth of your seed, and ye shall be his servants.
Montesquieu gave the constitutional idea its modern form: when the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, there can be no liberty.
The hope is for a “constitutional legitimate government … fully established”. Locke: where there is no law, there is no freedom.
When the banner of Constitution was raised “every one became hopeful”. Wordsworth on the first days of the French Revolution: bliss was it in that dawn to be alive.
Dickens opens his novel of the same revolution with both halves: it was the best of times, it was the worst of times. Which half do the readings record?
Repeated attempts to form consultative assemblies bore little fruit. Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.

Bahá’ís were at one point urged to seek election to the National Assembly. Burke told his electors what such a body is: not a congress of ambassadors from hostile interests, but a deliberative assembly of one nation, with one interest, that of the whole.
The Bahá’ís’ purpose is the Most Great Peace. They shall beat their swords into plowshares.
The friends “must not in any way discuss or interfere in such matters”. My kingdom is not of this world: if it were, then would my servants fight.

Douglass: those who profess to favor freedom and yet deprecate agitation want crops without plowing up the ground. A reformer of his kind would call non-interference a way of taking sides. What is the readings’ answer?
You were well-wishers of all and strove for reconciliation. Blessed are the peacemakers.
Both sides were counselled. Jefferson, taking office after a bitter election: every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle; we are all republicans, we are all federalists.
Admonitions were given to both sides, and neighbours meddled. In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not.
“So great a storm and convulsion” in so short a time. Yeats in 1919: things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; mere anarchy is loosed upon the world.
No agriculture, no trade, quarrels in every province. In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
Both sides have “washed their hands” of wisdom. Washington warned his country in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party.
The upheaval is traced to the deeds of particular clerics and oppressors. They have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.

The Bahá’ís were portrayed to each faction as partisans of the other. John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, He hath a devil; the Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous.
A Bahá’í “absolutely does not interfere in worldly affairs”. Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s.
The movement, the reading says, sprang from divines seeking to increase their dominion. Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.

The reading doubts the movement’s motives. The American Declaration holds that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, and that a people may alter them. Can a cause be just though some who lead it are not?

“They seek ruin while calling it prosperity; they desire bondage while naming it freedom.” Tacitus gives a British chieftain the classic line on such naming: they make a desert, and they call it peace.
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness.
A bomb was thrown at the Shah. All they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.

The king meant well; “the foolish ones” imagined reform possible through sedition. Burke, the great critic of revolution, also said that a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation. Where were the means of change in Qajar Persia?
If religious scholars interfere in politics, the result is ruin. Jefferson read his country’s first amendment as building a wall of separation between Church and State.
How could a ruined country, “people completely ignorant of law”, suddenly sustain a constitution? Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child.
Mill puts the point as a principle: the worth of a State, in the long run, is the worth of the individuals composing it.
It would have been better to proceed by degrees. First the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.
Now is the time for subjects to strive with sincerity and obedience. Paul asks prayers for kings and all in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life.
Peter and the apostles answered a council: we ought to obey God rather than men. The readings counsel obedience to a government that had killed Bahá’ís. Where is the limit, and who draws it?
These difficulties “will be resolved”. Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
The revolution will continue for a time, but its end will be good. I know the thoughts that I think toward you, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
Iran in time to come will be like a shining star. He will make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the Lord.

shortfall: Several readings repeat one sentence (that government and people must mix like milk and honey) or report particular events and persons; they share companions or have none.
